These hypotheses come from prior knowledge of NAS-Bench-201 behavior, since no results are available. The main reasoning is that edits adding a conv gain more when the cell is otherwise weakly connected, and they gain less once an alternative path already exists.

1. Setting edge 3 (the direct input-to-output edge) to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when it replaces `none` than when it replaces another op. Adding a path from nothing is a large gain, whereas replacing an existing op is a smaller change.
2. Setting edge 0 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 0 is `none` than when it is anything else. Connecting the input to node 1 opens up the whole 0->1->2/3 path.
3. Setting edge 5 to nor_conv_3x3 helps more when edge 5 is `none`. Without edge 5, node 2 is disconnected from the output.
4. Setting edge 3 to skip_connect helps more when edge 3 is `none`. A skip path adds a gradient shortcut where there was nothing.
5. Setting edge 5 to `none` hurts more (so the effect is lower) when edge 3 is `none`. Removing edge 5 then leaves fewer remaining routes to the output.
6. Setting edge 4 to `none` hurts more when edge 3 is `none`. Fewer routes to the output remain, so the loss is larger.
7. Setting edge 3 to `none` hurts more when edge 4 is `none`. The output then depends on edge 5 alone.
8. Setting edge 2 to skip_connect gives a lower effect when edge 2 is currently nor_conv_1x1, because replacing a conv with a skip loses capacity. It gives a higher effect when edge 2 is `none`.
9. Setting edge 0 to avg_pool_3x3 gives a higher effect when edge 0 is `none` than when it is a conv. This is the same connectivity argument as hypothesis 2, but with a weaker op.
10. Setting edge 0 to skip_connect gives a lower effect when edge 0 is nor_conv_3x3, because replacing the strongest op on the first edge costs accuracy.
